# Teaching a New Colleague: Passing On Practical Skills in the Workshop

Teaching someone a practical job is one of the most valuable things an experienced worker can do, yet it is also one of the most frequently done badly. In a workshop, where hands, tools, and machines meet, the difference between a well-taught task and a poorly explained one can be measured in wasted material, damaged equipment, or even injury. When a new colleague arrives, the responsibility of passing on knowledge falls to those who already know the work. The best approach follows a simple but disciplined sequence: demonstrate one complete task from start to finish, explain the reasoning behind each decision as you go, hand the task over to the learner, resist the urge to correct every small difference, distinguish between safety-critical steps and personal habits, leave behind usable notes, and finally check understanding by working through a fresh example together.

## Start with One Complete Task

The most common mistake in practical training is teaching in fragments. A new colleague shown a bit of filing, a bit of measuring, and a bit of assembly, all in separate pieces, never sees how the parts connect into a whole.
